significance.justification: Verified true, the conclusion would be that "subject-position enrichment binds attributes in one direction only" and that a measurable directional-decoding asymmetry predicts reverse-recall failure; this combines a form-(ii) causal account with a form-(iii) predictive coupling between the asymmetry index, relation directionality, and behavior. It would establish both a phenomenon—naturally bidirectional relations should show less reversal asymmetry—and a mechanism distinguishing directional access failure from general absence of factual knowledge, thereby fixing expected internal and behavioral outcomes across relation classes; this distinction bears directly on the failure documented by Berglund et al. in the ICLR 2024 Reversal Curse paper and on interpretations of subject-localized factual recall from Meng et al.'s causal-tracing work. The claim is determinate, and a negative result would rule out the specific subject-locus, one-way-binding explanation, although it would not rule out other access-based mechanisms. Topic substitution fails: the broad topic alone would not license this specific cross-relation predictive coupling or storage-versus-access explanation, supporting a score above the topic median.

reach.justification: The named handle is "the decodability asymmetry as a quantitative index of the curse," supplemented by the intervention that "explicitly writes the reverse association" through reverse-statement fine-tuning. The index is potentially ex ante because the claim says it can "predict which relations and training interventions can mitigate it," allowing relations to be screened before relying on reverse retrieval, rather than merely explaining errors afterward. After per-model re-extraction, the substantive prediction survives as a relation—greater directional asymmetry should imply worse reverse recall, while bidirectional text exposure should reduce both—under the hypothesis's asserted scope across models and factual relation classes; this could guide model auditors and training practitioners, though it is not a model-independent ready-made direction. Topic substitution again fails: without the asymmetry index, directional prediction, and mitigation rule, the topic supplies no comparable transferable handle.
